title: Three conventions make skills attributable without new agent capabilities
content:
## Claim

Attributable skill execution does not require new agent capabilities. It requires three conventions:

1. Skills declare the document models they operate on and the actions they may emit
2. The agent runtime dispatches skill outputs as actions, not raw text or unstructured tool calls
3. Artifacts are document-model documents (schema + operation log)

## Cost vs payoff

Modest discipline at the skill/runtime boundary; structural payoff for evaluation (process auditing), safety (attribution), and knowledge claims (falsifiability via "how was this made?").

## Methodology grounding
The claims below live in the plugin's `data/methodology/` corpus; the relationship is stated per claim.

- **[[hook enforcement guarantees quality while instruction enforcement merely suggests it]]** — BUILDS_ON. The three conventions are enforcement dressed as convention: they hold without asking the model for a new capability, which is the same reason the methodology prefers a hook to an instruction.
- **[[agent session boundaries create natural automation checkpoints that human-operated systems lack]]** — RELATES_TO. Conventions that fire at an invocation boundary need no memory to be reliable, which is the property that claim identifies as the agent architecture's accidental advantage.
description: Skills declare models and actions; runtimes dispatch actions not raw text; artifacts are document-model documents with schemas and logs.
